item.title: Hydrogen isotopes reveal water leakage from the core
item.dc:creator: Yu Zhang
Wenzhong Wang
Zhongqing Wu
Bowen Chen
item.description: Chemical heterogeneities in Earth’s deep mantle may record either preserved primordial reservoirs or later core-mantle exchange, but distinguishing between these origins remains challenging. Hydrogen isotopes offer a sensitive tracer, yet whether magma ocean crystallization could generate a deuterium-depleted deep reservoir has not been quantitatively evaluated. Here, we use machine learning–accelerated path-integral simulations to determine equilibrium hydrogen isotope fractionation between silicate melt and bridgmanite, ringwoodite, and wadsleyite under magma ocean conditions. Incorporating these fractionation factors into a magma ocean crystallization model shows that mineral-melt fractionation is intrinsically weak, producing an essentially homogeneous D/H distribution in the primitive mantle. Magma ocean crystallization therefore cannot generate the extremely low δD values observed in some ocean island basalts. Combined with exceptionally high 3 He/ 4 He ratios, these signatures more plausibly reflect selective transfer of primordial volatiles from Earth’s core, implying sustained volatile exchange across the core-mantle boundary. item.dc:creator: Ze-Zhou Wang

item.description: Deep recycling of surficial carbonates into the mantle may play a critical role in shaping Earth’s long-term habitability, yet its contribution to the deep mantle carbon budget remains uncertain. Magnesium isotopes provide a promising tracer for addressing this issue, because of the uniquely light isotopic signatures of sedimentary carbonates. Here, we present high-precision magnesium isotopic compositions (δ 26 Mg) for 152 globally distributed plume-related lavas sampling diverse mantle end-members. We find that δ 26 Mg values below the bulk silicate Earth range are commonly associated with increasingly pronounced radiogenic isotopic signatures indicative of recycled crustal components. These features are best explained by the incorporation of isotopically light magnesium derived from subducted carbonate-bearing crustal materials into their mantle sources. On the basis of these observations, the lower mantle is estimated to contain up to ∼130 or ∼230–parts per million recycled carbon, potentially constituting a substantial portion of its total carbon budget. item.title: The riverine land-to-ocean carbon flux
item.dc:creator: Robert G. M. Spencer
Travis W. Drake
Maodian Liu
Peter A. Raymond
item.description: The land-to-ocean export of carbon via rivers is a key component in the global carbon cycle. In this Review, we provide an overview of the factors governing the mobilization of carbon into rivers and those modulating riverine carbon export to the ocean. Terrestrial landscapes are estimated to deliver 3–4 PgC yr^−1 to inland waters, with the majority outgassed rather than exported to the ocean. Model estimates converge on a total global carbon export flux of 0.8–1.0 PgC yr^−1; however, regional, watershed and carbon species resolved estimates vary substantially owing to differences in source inputs, transport processes, biogeochemical transformations, and climate and hydrological drivers. Across the models that were synthesized, global estimates for individual carbon species span approximately a threefold difference, whereas estimated export of some species to the Atlantic and Pacific basins varies by up to fivefold. The Amazon and Congo together contribute approximately 21% of global river discharge, yet remain far less observed than many smaller temperate watersheds; the world’s 30 largest rivers by discharge account for approximately half of global cumulative river discharge. Therefore, expanding observations is clearly a priority to reduce uncertainties in modelled land-to-ocean carbon fluxes, and could be supported by the development of sensor networks and remote sensing observations to improve spatiotemporal resolution. Integrating these large datasets with mechanistic studies of biogeochemical modulators and machine learning approaches would inform understanding of carbon dynamics within major watersheds and improve predictions of this globally important carbon flux. Globally, rivers export ~10^15 grams of carbon to the ocean each year. This Review explores the mobilization, modulation and transport of different species of carbon within watersheds and rivers, with the aim to help inform and improve land-to-ocean carbon flux estimates. item.description: Episodic lava fountaining is rare globally, with only three occurrences from Kīlauea (Hawaii) since 1823. item.description: Nitrogen regulates primary productivity across much of the biosphere, yet fixed nitrogen loss remains poorly constrained because existing methods rely on indirect proxies or ex situ experiments. item.description: The mechanism driving accelerating unrest at the densely populated Campi Flegrei caldera since 2005 remains debated. Analyzing an unprecedented two-decade geochemical dataset, we show that escalating soil CO 2 fluxes closely tracks caldera uplift, revealing magmatic fluid pressurization at 3- to 4-kilometer depth and heating as the fundamental driver of the unrest. A critical magmatic gas pulse occurred between 2018 and 2022 specifically focused this outgassing beneath the Solfatara crater. Thermodynamic modeling demonstrates that an increasing mass of ascending fluid pressurizes the hydrothermal system, forcing vapor condensation within the upper kilometer. This condensation transfers latent heat to the crust. We calculate that this released thermal energy is an order of magnitude greater than that required for the 1.6-meter uplift since 2005. Ultimately, this fluid pressurization and heating drive accelerating deformation and seismicity; alongside the 2021 emergence of seismic sequences with short inter-event times, it directly signals an escalating phreatic or magmatic eruption risk. item.dc:creator: Hugo Delile

item.description: How mining has shaped long-term economic and political landscapes across Europe and the Mediterranean remains poorly understood, largely because archaeological evidence is spatially fragmented and ore sources are difficult to trace from atmospheric lead (Pb) records. Here, we compile Pb isotope data from environmental archives and introduce the Environmental Match Intensity Index (EMII), a metric applied to peat records to track Pb–silver (Ag) ore-supply patterns and relative changes in the integrated mining-related atmospheric Pb signal over six millennia. EMII reveals an early mining signal centered on Laurion (Greece) during the Late Neolithic/Chalcolithic, followed by Bronze Age expansion structured by maritime routes linking the Cyclades, the Troad, and Anatolian coasts. From the Iron Age onward, our results challenge the conventional Iberian-centered mining model and instead reveal a polycentric and multimodal organization rooted in west-central European districts interconnected through major fluvial corridors and complementary terrestrial and maritime routes. EMII reaches its first major peak during the Early Roman period, declines during Late Antiquity and the Early Middle Ages, and rises again from the High Middle Ages onward. Despite these temporal fluctuations, the overall continental distribution of the contributing mining regions remains broadly stable. By connecting environmental archives with mining, transport, and urban demand, this framework provides a scalable approach for reconstructing the long-term organization of metal production and circulation and their contribution to anthropization processes across different chrono-cultural periods and geographical settings. item.description: Abstract Bridgmanite, the main mineralogical phase in the Earth’s lower mantle, is intrinsically anisotropic and may therefore generate seismic anisotropy in actively-deforming regions, particularly subduction zones. The bulk of the lower mantle is widely regarded as well-mixed but recent seismic observations suggest structures at mid-mantle depths whose origin remains unclear. Here, we propose a mechanism that could generate seismic discontinuities beneath subduction zones with depth distributions consistent with some of the observed mid-mantle reflectors. By coupling thermo-mechanical subduction models with pressure-dependent fabric calculations, we show that gradual slip transitions in bridgmanite with depth can manifest anisotropic discontinuities near 1000 km, which can deepen depending on the extent of accumulated deformation. This discontinuity is most pronounced in regions of strong slab-driven flow as revealed by its reflection coefficients, the strength of which varies with distance and azimuth. While our models predict ~ 1.5% contrast in fast versus slow shear wave velocities in terms of radial anisotropy, our full waveform simulations show that the discontinuity is detectable with array seismological methods. These results suggest that mid-mantle reflectors near subduction zones may be strain-induced, providing an additional mechanism that links mantle flow, mineral physics, and seismic observations. item.title: Interaction of siderite with sulfur-rich fluids at mantle as a model for diamond formation in the Precambrian
item.dc:creator: Yuliya V. Bataleva

item.description: Fe-rich carbonates (siderite and ankerite) of banded iron formations (BIF) are considered as a potential carbon source to produce diamonds during subduction in Mesoarchean to Paleoproterozoic. Here, we experimentally demonstrate that diamond nucleation and subsequent growth can occur via the interaction of siderite, originated from subducted BIFs, with sulfur-rich mantle fluids under pressure of 6.3 GPa and temperatures of 1450–1550 °C, corresponding to Archean subduction geotherm. Under these conditions, Fe,Ca,Mg-carbonate melt with dissolved sulfur can probably act as both diamond formation medium and carbon source, and the driving forces for diamond growth might be the redox reactions of carbonate and sulfide melts. Resulting diamonds are predominantly octahedral, contain 300–900 ppm nitrogen, host sulfide, graphite, carbonate and magnetite inclusions and display new vibronic systems with zero-phonon lines at 429 and 693 nm, which are most likely associated with S- and Fe-related defects in the diamond lattice. We demonstrate that diamond growth rate and the number of inclusions increases with increasing iron content of the carbonate melt with dissolved sulfur. These features provide diagnostic criteria for natural diamonds with magnetite inclusions and specific defect-impurity characteristics. We developed a model of Precambrian diamond formation in subducted carbonated BIFs, that consists of the sequential implementation of processes: (1) sulfidation of siderite, (2) siderite partial decomposition with magnetite +C0 + O2/CO2 formation, and (3) diamond-producing redox interactions between Fe,Mg,Ca,Mn-carbonate melt and sulfide melt. item.description: The early India-Eurasia collision induced widespread tectonic deformation and vigorous magmatism throughout southern Tibet, yet the dynamic connections between magmatism and crustal evolution in the collision zone remain controversial. item.description: The Cunqian Cu-Pb-Zn deposit is a significant skarn-porphyry deposit located at the junction of the eastern and central segments of the Qin-Hang metallogenic belt (QHMB) in China. Hf isotopic compositions (εHf(t) = –9.8 to –6.7) and corresponding two-stage model ages (TDM2 = 1.6–1.9 Ga) of the same zircon population indicate derivation mainly from recycled Paleoproterozoic crustal components. Numerous inherited zircon cores (417–3102 Ma) are present, and the ca. 817 Ma group is particularly noteworthy for its elevated εHf(t) values (3.4–7.4), which indicate involvement of Neoproterozoic juvenile crustal components in the source region. Zircon trace elements indicate that the ore-related magmas exhibited moderately oxidized conditions (mean ΔFMQ = 0.94) and elevated magmatic water contents (7.92–11.0 wt.%), suggesting their formation from an oxidized and hydrous magma. Fertile magmatism derived from crustal sources may therefore favor Pb-Zn-rich mineralization even under oxidizing conditions, possibly reflecting magmatic evolution processes that limited Cu enrichment. The Cunqian deposit underscores the considerable Cu-Pb-Zn exploration potential of such transitional zones, where polymetallic mineralization associated with ancient crustal reworking is preferentially localized. item.description: Granite-related Sn–W polymetallic deposits represent a major global source of Sn and W, yet the mechanisms driving their co-enrichment with chalcophile elements (e.g., Cu, Ag) remain poorly understood. Along the southwestern margin of the South China Block, four equally spaced magmatic suites, ranging from Early Paleozoic to Cretaceous in age and from granitic to mafic in composition, host large to giant Sn–W polymetallic deposits with diverse metal associations, providing an ideal natural laboratory to address this issue. By integrating new and published geochronological and geochemical data, we identify four magmatic pulses during both the Early Paleozoic (442.2–402.4 Ma) and the Cretaceous (117.1–77.4 Ma). Based on ages and metal associations, the ore-related intrusions are classified into four groups: (1) Sn–W-related Cretaceous peraluminous granites; (2) Ag-related Cretaceous metaluminous to weakly peraluminous granites; (3) Sn–W–Cu-related Early Paleozoic mafic–granitic rocks; and (4) Sn–Cu-related Cretaceous mafic–granitic rocks. These granite types display distinct elemental and isotopic signatures, reflecting diverse origins and evolutionary processes: (1) Sn–W-related granites formed via mica (muscovite and biotite)-dehydration melting of Proterozoic metapelites; (2) Ag-related granites derived from amphibole-dehydration melting of Proterozoic amphibolites; (3) Sn–W–Cu-related granites originated from mica-dehydration melting of Proterozoic metapelites with additional input from asthenospheric mantle-derived mafic magmas; and (4) Sn–Cu-related granites stemmed from a similar metapelitic source but with contributions from enriched lithospheric mantle-derived mafic magmas. These petrogenetic models reveal that Sn–W-dominated mineralization is primarily linked to mica-dehydration melting of metapelites, whereas chalcophile element-dominated mineralization is associated with mantle-derived magmas or amphibole-dehydration melting of mafic lower crust derived from such magmas. item.description: The mechanisms of rare metal mineralization within highly evolved granite–pegmatite systems remain a topic of debate, particularly regarding the role of magmatic–hydrothermal processes in rare metal enrichment. It exhibits a progressive lithological transition from amazonite-free granite in the lower lithological zones (LLZ) to amazonite-rich granite and pegmatite veins in the middle lithological zones (MLZ) to amazonite-poor granite in the upper lithological zone (ULZ), which formed as a result of the magmatic–hydrothermal evolution of a single granitic melt. Accordingly, this pluton provides a unique opportunity to investigate the mechanisms of rare metal mineralization through quantitatively constraining the origin and physicochemical properties of fluids, and by evaluating how these fluids drive geochemical fractionation during magmatic–hydrothermal evolution. This is accomplished here by characterizing the δ18O values of microtexturally and chemically heterogeneous domains in zircon and quartz from the different lithological zones of the BST pluton. Magmatic zircon domains (Zrn-I; δ18OZrn-I = 5.88–7.39‰) have δ18O values that reflect that of the parental granitic melt. In contract, quartz phenocrysts (δ18OQtz = 8.71–10.97‰) and hydrothermal zircon domains (Zrn-II and Zrn-III; δ18OZrn-II = 6.67–12.18‰; δ18OZrn-III = 15.03–20.69‰) exhibit systematically elevated δ18O values. item.description: Subducting slabs in the mantle transition zone (MTZ) exhibit complex deformation patterns and host deep-focus earthquakes. Two long-standing puzzles concern why some slabs stagnate near the 660-km discontinuity while others penetrate into the lower mantle, and how earthquake-like failure can occur under the high-pressure conditions of the deep mantle. A key process linking these phenomena is the metastable transformation of olivine to its high-pressure polymorphs within cold slab interiors. Kinetic inhibition of this transition can lead to the formation of a metastable olivine wedge (MOW), which modifies slab buoyancy, releases latent heat, and produces fine-grained microstructures. Laboratory experiments and seismic observations provide strong evidence for the existence of MOWs, yet the dynamic consequences of the buoyancy and grain-size changes on slab morphology, kinematics, and long-term evolution have not been explored in self-consistent dynamic models. Here we show that incorporating fully coupled metastable kinetics with both grain-boundary nucleation and interface-controlled grain growth, together with grain-size–dependent composite rheology, fundamentally alters subduction dynamics in both 2-D and 3-D free-subduction models. When transition kinetics reduce grain size within the slab interior, our simulations predict that the MOW persistently extends deeper than 550 km for an 80 Ma slab. The resulting time-dependent buoyancy suppresses slab folding above the MOW by buffering subducting-plate velocities, whereas the small grain size promotes folding below the MOW through rheological weakening. In addition, models with both a MOW and grain-size evolution strongly promote trench retreat and the development of trench curvature. Together, these results demonstrate that metastable kinetics and grain-size evolution provide a unifying framework for linking microscopic phase-transition processes to macroscopic slab dynamics, offering new insight into slab morphology and the physical conditions governing deep-focus earthquakes. item.description: The systematic spatial differentiation of metals within a single stratigraphic framework is a defining feature of strata-bound mineral systems, yet the physical processes that drive such zonation remain poorly constrained. Steep solubility gradients of CuCl2 − focus copper precipitation in high-temperature zones (≤ 350 °C) proximal to the heat source, while the relative stability of Au(HS)2 − facilitates gold transport to distal mixing fronts. item.description: Abstract The Tailaihua Nb–Ta–Be deposit in the southern Great Xing’an Range, Northeast China, is hosted in a highly fractionated peraluminous albite granite. New monazite U–Pb dating yields an emplacement age of ca. 147 Ma, and positive eNd(t) values with young two-stage Nd model ages indicate derivation by partial melting of Phanerozoic juvenile crust. Whole-rock geochemistry reveals extreme enrichment in SiO₂ and Rb, strong depletion in Sr, Ba, and Eu, and pronounced rare-earth element tetrad effects, together with widespread replacement textures in muscovite and columbite-group minerals (CGM), documenting intense fractional crystallization and melt–fluid interaction during magmatic–hydrothermal evolution. Niobium–tantalum mineralization is dominated by magmatic and magmatic–hydrothermal transition processes. Early CGM cores formed via fractional crystallization of evolved granitic melt, whereas Ta-rich rims record overgrowth and modification by interacting residual melt and exsolved fluids during the magmatic–hydrothermal transition. Tungsten mineralization occurs in three successive generations: W-rich fluid replacement of early CGM forms wolframoixiolite and Nb–Ta-rich wolframite (Wlf-1); intensive water–rock interaction precipitates greisen-hosted wolframite (Wlf-2); and decreasing P–T in fractures generates quartz–wolframite veins (Wlf-3) during the post-magmatic hydrothermal stage. Identical core–rim CGM textures in both granite and greisen demonstrate that large-scale fluid exsolution initiated early during granitic melt evolution, overlapping temporally with fractional crystallization and melt–fluid interaction, rather than occurring as a discrete late-stage event. The timing of fluid exsolution from melt represents a key control on the Nb–Ta mineralizing potential of exsolved fluids. This study provides a general model for Nb–Ta mineralization applicable to W–Be-mineralized albite granite systems.
